procedural_history.originating_court: A trial court (as evidenced by the existence of FIR No. 113 of 2017)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 02.12.2020 of the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in CRLP No.8003 of 2019
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed a petition under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) before the High Court of Karnataka, seeking to quash FIR No. 113 of 2017. Their argument was that the FIR was primarily a civil dispute with no criminal element and an abuse of process. The High Court dismissed their petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants (Assistant Manager (Marketing) and the Managing Director of a bicycle manufacturing company) appealed to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order dated 02.12.2020. They argued that the FIR instituted by Respondent No. 2 (the complainant) was primarily a civil dispute with no criminal element and an abuse of process. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the High Court dated 02.12.2020 and quashed the criminal proceedings arising out of FIR No.113 of 2017.

directions: Set aside the order of the High Court dated 02.12.2020.
The criminal proceedings arising out of FIR No.113 of 2017 will hereby stand quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to quash criminal proceedings arising out of a civil transaction, especially after the dispute had been settled between the parties.

facts: A commercial dispute arose between the appellants and Respondent No. 2 over payments for services rendered.
Respondent No. 2 filed an FIR against the appellants for cheating and criminal breach of trust.
After the FIR was filed, the parties reached a settlement where the appellants paid an additional INR 26,00,000 to Respondent No. 2 as a full and final settlement, which the respondent accepted.

The High Court refused to quash the criminal proceedings, reasoning that the appellants' payment of an amount higher than they initially claimed to owe was prima facie evidence of an intention to cheat from the beginning.
law: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the High Court has inherent powers to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the court's process or to secure the ends of justice.
This power should be exercised when a dispute that is essentially civil in nature is given the "cloak of a criminal offence."
A mere breach of contract does not automatically constitute a criminal offence.
To establish the crime of cheating, it must be proven that there was a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the very beginning of the transaction, not just a subsequent failure to fulfill a promise.
application: The Supreme Court identified the dispute as being "essentially of a civil nature," stemming from a breach of contract.
The Court found that the subsequent settlement, where an additional payment was made and accepted, was a crucial factor that the High Court failed to properly consider.

It rejected the High Court's logic, stating that the additional amount paid as part of the settlement cannot be presumed to be an act of cheating. Instead, it was an effort to give a "quietus to the whole situation."
The Court concluded that there was no criminal element present and that continuing the prosecution after the settlement constituted an "abuse of the process" of the court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in refusing to quash the criminal proceedings. It held that this was a clear case where the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC, as the dispute was civil in nature and had been settled between the parties. Therefore, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the criminal proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be exercised to quash criminal proceedings when a dispute, which is essentially civil in nature, is given the cloak of a criminal offense.

facts: The case involved a commercial dispute between the appellants (employees of a bicycle company) and Respondent No. 2, who was contracted to assemble and transport bicycles.
A dispute arose over payments, leading Respondent No. 2 to file an FIR for cheating and criminal breach of trust.
Subsequently, the parties reached a settlement where the appellants paid an additional INR 26,00,000 to Respondent No. 2, which was accepted as a full and final settlement.
Despite the settlement, a chargesheet was filed, and the appellants petitioned the High Court to quash the proceedings, arguing the dispute was civil in nature.
The High Court refused to quash the FIR, believing a prima facie case was made out.
law: The Supreme Court relied on Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), which grants High Courts inherent power to prevent the abuse of the court's process and secure the ends of justice.

It cited the precedent set in *Paramjeet Batra v. State of Uttarakhand*, which held that while this power should be used sparingly, a High Court must not hesitate to quash criminal proceedings for disputes that are essentially civil in nature but are given the 'cloak of a criminal offence'.

The Court also referenced legal principles establishing that a mere breach of contract does not automatically constitute a criminal offense (*Sarabjit Kaur v. State of Punjab*) and that to prove cheating, a fraudulent or dishonest intention must exist from the very beginning of the transaction (*Vesa Holdings (P) Ltd. v. State of Kerala*).
application: The Supreme Court determined that the dispute was fundamentally a breach of contract, which is a civil matter.
It found that not only was the dispute civil, but it had also been resolved through a settlement, with the respondent accepting a substantial payment.
The Court rejected the respondent's later claim that the settlement was coerced, noting the absence of any complaint or FIR regarding coercion at the time.
It disagreed with the High Court's reasoning, stating that the additional amount paid as part of the settlement could not be interpreted as evidence of an initial intent to cheat.
The Court concluded that there was no criminal element present and that allowing the criminal proceedings to continue would be a clear abuse of the process of the court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court should have exercised its inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash the criminal proceedings. It held that since the dispute was essentially civil in nature and had been subsequently settled by the parties, continuing the criminal case was an abuse of the legal process. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and quashed the FIR and all related criminal proceedings.

issue.issue_text: Whether a mere breach of contract, without proof of a fraudulent or dishonest intention to cheat from the beginning, can attract criminal prosecution for cheating.

facts: The dispute originated from a contract where the appellants engaged respondent No. 2 to assemble and deliver bicycles.
A disagreement arose over the amount owed, with respondent No. 2 claiming he was underpaid, leading him to file an FIR for cheating and criminal breach of trust.
After the FIR was filed, the parties entered into a Compromise Deed, and the appellants paid an additional Rs. 26 lakhs as a full and final settlement, which was accepted by respondent No. 2.
Respondent No. 2 later claimed this settlement was coerced.

The High Court refused to quash the criminal proceedings, reasoning that the appellants' payment of an amount higher than what they initially claimed to owe was evidence of a fraudulent intention from the beginning.
law: To constitute the offence of cheating, it must be proven that the accused had a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise.
A mere breach of contract does not automatically give rise to a criminal offence of cheating.

High Courts have the inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash criminal proceedings that are essentially civil disputes cloaked in a criminal offence, in order to prevent the abuse of the legal process.
application: The Supreme Court identified the core of the dispute as being civil and contractual in nature.

The Court disagreed with the High Court's interpretation of the settlement payment. It held that the additional amount paid was part of a settlement to "give a quietus to the whole situation" and bring peace, not an admission of guilt or proof of an initial intent to cheat.
The Court found the allegation of a coerced settlement to be unlikely, as respondent No. 2 had duly accepted the payment and had not filed any separate FIR or complaint alleging coercion.

Applying the established legal principle, the Court found that the essential ingredient for cheating—a fraudulent or dishonest intention from the outset—was absent. The case was merely a breach of contract that had been subsequently settled.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since the dispute was civil in nature and there was no evidence of a fraudulent or dishonest intention from the beginning, a criminal prosecution for cheating was not sustainable. The Court held that the criminal proceedings were an abuse of process and quashed the FIR and all related proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in refusing to quash criminal proceedings arising out of a civil transaction, especially after the dispute had been settled between the parties.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in refusing to quash the criminal proceedings because the underlying dispute is a civil transaction concerning non-payment for services rendered.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's refusal to quash was justified because the appellants' failure to pay the full invoiced amount (paying only Rs. 35,37,390/- against an invoice of Rs. 1,01,58,574/-) constitutes criminal breach of trust and cheating, not merely a civil dispute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be exercised to quash criminal proceedings when a dispute, which is essentially civil in nature, is given the cloak of a criminal offense.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC should have been exercised to quash the proceedings to prevent the abuse of the criminal justice process and to secure the ends of justice, as this is a civil dispute disguised as a criminal case.
respondent_arguments: The High Court correctly refrained from exercising its inherent powers as the facts disclose a prima facie criminal offense of cheating and breach of trust, not just a civil dispute.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a mere breach of contract, without proof of a fraudulent or dishonest intention to cheat from the beginning, can attract criminal prosecution for cheating.
appellant_arguments: The dispute over non-payment is a breach of contract and does not amount to the criminal offense of cheating, as there is no evidence of a fraudulent or dishonest intention from the inception of the agreement.
respondent_arguments: The failure to pay the due amount after the services were rendered is not a mere breach of contract but an act of cheating and criminal breach of trust, justifying criminal prosecution.

cases.case_name: Paramjeet Batra v. State of Uttarakhand
cases.principle: Although the inherent powers of a High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be exercised sparingly, the High Court must not hesitate in quashing criminal proceedings which are essentially of a civil nature.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court must not hesitate to exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash criminal proceedings that are essentially of a civil nature, especially when a civil remedy is available and has been adopted, in order to prevent the abuse of the court's process.
obiter: The power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be exercised sparingly.
A complaint disclosing civil transactions may also have a criminal texture.
Whether a complaint discloses a criminal offence or not depends upon the nature of facts alleged therein.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The dispute between the parties was essentially of a civil nature relating to a breach of contract, and it also stood settled subsequently. In the absence of any criminal element or proof that a fraudulent or dishonest intention to cheat existed at the time of making the promise, continuing the criminal proceedings is nothing but an abuse of the process of the court.
legal_tests_applied: When exercising inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court must see whether a dispute which is essentially of a civil nature is given a cloak of criminal offence, and if so, it should not hesitate to quash the criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of process of the court.

To establish the criminal offense of cheating, as distinct from a mere breach of contract, it is required to be shown that the accused had a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise.
why_respondent_won: The dispute was essentially of a civil nature, concerning a breach of contract, which had been given the cloak of a criminal offense.
A mere breach of contract, by one of the parties, would not attract prosecution for a criminal offense in every case.
There was no evidence to show that the appellants had a fraudulent or dishonest intention to cheat at the inception of the contract.
The dispute between the parties had already been settled, which further demonstrated its civil nature and made the continuation of criminal proceedings an abuse of process.

The High Court erred in failing to exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash proceedings that were an abuse of the process and to secure the ends of justice.
policy_considerations: The inherent powers under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code exist to stop the abuse of the process of any court and to secure the ends of justice.
The High Court must not hesitate in quashing criminal proceedings which are essentially of a civil nature to prevent the misuse of criminal proceedings as a weapon of harassment.
Courts must prevent civil disputes from being given a 'cloak of criminal offence,' especially when a civil remedy is available and has been adopted.
